**To Reviewer En71**

Thank you for the insightful and positive comments. In the following, we provide our point-by-point response and hope our response helps address your concerns. We also look forward to the subsequent discussion which further helps to solve the current issues.

> **Q1: Extend to Deformation-Like Edits.**

**A1:** Thank you for the insightful suggestion. Our main experiments focus on the most common 3D editing operations (add, remove, and replace) where the edited regions exhibit clear and localized structural or appearance variations. This experimental scope aligns with established 3D editing benchmarks and SoTA baselines (e.g., EditP23 , Instant3dit , and VoxHammer), which similarly prioritize semantic replacement and topological modification over continuous geometric deformation. Although we did not explicitly benchmark deformation-like edits as a separate category, our framework can generalizes to some deformation scenarios. 

To further illustrate this capability, we have added examples of deformation-like edits on https://anonymousresearch37.github.io/3DEditFormer/ (videos 4-5) and Figure 11 in the revised Appendix, such as "make the dog's limbs shorter and its body plumper" or "make the tree grows straight". These qualitative results show that 3DEditFormer can produce coherent structural adaptations for deformation-like edits, indicating that the model is not limited to part manipulation but can also accommodate smooth geometric transformations.

We agree that a systematic evaluation of deformation-centric edits is an exciting direction, and we plan to expand 3DEditVerse in future work to include richer deformation annotations.

> **Q2: On the use of Trellis's two diffusion modules.**

**A2:** We appreciate the reviewer’s observation. Our framework, like Trellis, utilizes both diffusion modules: (1) the voxel-generation transformer and (2) the structured-latent refinement transformer.

For simplicity, the high-level overview in Fig. 3 presents the architecture in a unified form, but in practice, consistent with Section 4.4, each stage is equipped with its own Dual-Guidance Attention blocks and is trained independently following the original two-stage procedure.

Concretely:

(1) Voxel stage: responsible for large-scale geometric adaptation and establishing globally coherent shape changes.

(2) Latent-refinement stage: responsible for refining fine-grained geometry and appearance while preserving the structural information of the source asset.

This two-stage formulation is essential: voxel-level editing provides coarse geometric consistency, and structured-latent refinement ensures high-quality texture and detail alignment with the target image.

> **Q3: Inference time consumption.**

**A3:** We have added an inference-time comparison to the revised version. For a single edit, executed on a L40s GPU, the runtime is:

| Method | Runtime (s) |
| - | - |
| EditP23 | 9.8 |
| Instant3Dit | 16.7 |
| VoxHammer | 69.8 |
| 3DEditFormer (Ours) | 19.8 |

As shown above, our method achieves 19.8 s per edit on an L40s GPU, which is comparable to EditP23 and Instant3Dit while being far more efficient than VoxHammer. Importantly, VoxHammer requires precise 3D masks, whereas 3DEditFormer performs editing in a single forward pass without any mask, making the overall pipeline more practical.

> **Q4: On the meaning of "Consistent" in the title.**

**A4:** Thank you for pointing this out. The term "Consistent" in our title refers to two complementary notions of consistency:

(1) Semantic Edit Consistency:
Whether the edited result faithfully aligns with the user-specified target image or instruction. This reflects how accurately the edit is realized.

(2) Structure-Preserving Consistency:
Whether regions outside the edited area maintain the original geometry and appearance of the source 3D asset. This captures cross-view geometric stability and edit locality.

Both forms of consistency are quantitatively reflected in our 2D and 3D metrics in Table 2.

**To Reviewer 41EE**

Thank you for the insightful and positive comments. In the following, we provide our point-by-point response and hope our response helps address your concerns. We also look forward to the subsequent discussion which further helps to solve the current issues.

> **Q1: Scope of Pose-Driven Structural Edits.**

**A1:** Thank you for the comment. We acknowledge that the pose-driven subset primarily contains human-like characters because articulated human avatars are the most common assets in real creative workflows (games, animation, VR). For this reason, we focused on human-pose editing as a core scenario. 

However, we supplement qualitative experiments for animal characters (i.e., videos 1-3 of deer, eagle, and monkey) on https://anonymousresearch37.github.io/3DEditFormer/ and Figure 10 in the revised Appendix. Although our 3DEditFormer is trained on human-pose editing data, it can generalize naturally to non-human pose editing. 

As shown in the video demo on the webpage, 3DEditFormer successfully handles non-human articulations such as raising the head of an animal. These results indicate that our method extends beyond humanoid cases and can effectively handle pose-driven edits for a broader range of articulated objects.


> **Q2: Complexity and Stability of the Appearance-Driven Pipeline.**

**A2:** We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding complexity and stability of the appearance-driven pipeline. For the text-guided appearance edits, we implemented a strict filtering protocol at every stage, retaining only high-fidelity pairs:

* Prompt Generation: Starting with the 4,585-word Vocabulary Set from Tag2Text, we utilized DeepSeek-R1 to generate 20 diverse prompts per word, resulting in an initial pool of 91,700 text prompts.

* Image Generation & Editing: Source and target images were generated via Flux.1-Dev and Flux.1-Kontext, respectively. To filter out cases where the editing model failed to execute the instruction (resulting in near-identical images), we computed similarity scores and discarded pairs with negligible changes. (Remaining: 89,550).

* 3D Pair Initialization: Images were lifted to 3D using Trellis. Pairs where the source and target 3D assets remained identical in voxel space were removed, as they provided no useful geometric editing signal. (Remaining: 70,144).

* Mask Computation: We utilized Qwen-VL for edit localization. Samples where the model failed to detect a valid editing region (i.e., no bounding box returned) were discarded to guarantee successful 3D mask projection. (Remaining: 55,026).

* Consistency Filtering: Finally, we applied the Post-Editing Consistency Filtering (as detailed in Section 3) using multi-view DINOv2 similarity to eliminate inconsistent generations. (Final High-Quality Pairs: 43,874).

Consequently, the pipeline retains only 47.8% of the initial candidates, ensuring high reliability. Examples are shown in Figure 6 in the Appendix.

Finally, 3DEditVerse significantly outperforms prior benchmarks in both data volume and quality (Table 1):

* 3D-Alpaca-Editing (52,532 train / 0 test): Is less than half the size of our dataset and suffers from poor consistency because it independently generates "before" and "after" assets.

* CMD (40,000 train / 50 test): Is limited in scale and lacks semantic harmony, as it constructs edits by naively concatenating unrelated 3D objects.

* Edit3D-Bench (0 train / 300 test): Provides no training data and only a small test set, limiting its utility for learning-based approaches.

In contrast, 3DEditVerse (116,309 train / 1,500 test) is the largest paired 3D editing dataset to date (roughly $2\times$ larger than the nearest competitor). It is the first resource to simultaneously guarantee massive scale, edit locality, multi-view consistency, and semantic harmony, establishing a reliable foundation for training robust 3D editing models.

> **Q3: Missing Video Results.**

**A3:** Thank you for pointing this out. We do provide extensive video demonstrations of both baseline methods and our 3DEditFormer. As stated in the abstract, all video results are available on our project page: https://anonymousresearch37.github.io/3DEditFormer/.

In the Comparison section, users can view rotating video sequences for both our method and VoxHammer, and click on any sequence to enable free rotation, zooming, and close inspection of geometry and texture from arbitrary viewpoints. These interactive results verify that our edits maintain strong cross-view consistency and faithfully align with the target image.

Besides, to further address other reviewers’ concerns, we have additionally included video demonstrations for Deformation-like Editing, Non-Human Pose Editing, and Real-Object Editing. These examples provide broader evidence of the robustness and versatility of 3DEditFormer across a wide range of editing scenarios.

> **Q2: Dynamic 3d object (e.g. Diffusion4D) used for 3d editing.**

**A2:** We appreciate the reviewer pointing out the connection to dynamic 3D datasets like Diffusion4D. We analyze the relationship and the necessity of our approach below:

(1) Alignment with Pose-Driven Edits: The dynamic 3D assets used in Diffusion4D are essentially Objaverse objects annotated with dynamic motion labels, allowing different poses of the same 3D asset. This concept aligns closely with the Character–Animation Compositions subset of our 3DEditVerse, where we utilize animation frames of rigged characters to construct ground-truth pairs for pose-driven geometric editing.

(2) Limitation of Dynamic Assets: However, datasets based solely on dynamic sequences are fundamentally limited to articulation and deformation. They do not cover the broader spectrum of 3D editing tasks required in real-world workflows, specifically:

* Topological Changes: Adding or removing parts.

* Semantic Swaps: Replacing objects or components.

* Appearance Modifications: Changing textures or materials without altering geometry.

(3) The Necessity of 3DEditVerse: To address these gaps, 3DEditVerse is designed as a unified benchmark that complements pose-driven edits with a Text–Image–3D Lifting pipeline. This enables the generation of diverse appearance-driven and structural edits that cannot be derived from dynamic sequences alone. By covering both kinematic deformations and semantic/topological modifications, 3DEditVerse establishes a more comprehensive and practical standard for scalable 3D editing.


> **Q3: Writing coherence.**

**A3:** We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive feedback regarding the narrative flow. We acknowledge that presenting both a large-scale benchmark (3DEditVerse) and a novel architecture (3DEditFormer) within a single paper creates a dense structure. In the final version, we will enhance the writing coherence by more explicitly delineating the logical progression between the data and the model:

(1) Data Foundation (3DEditVerse): We will clarify how the dataset addresses the scarcity of paired 3D data through two complementary pipelines: Pose-Driven Geometric Edits (derived from animation sequences ) and Text-Guided Appearance Edits (generated via our multi-model lifting pipeline ).

(2) Methodological Solution (3DEditFormer): We will then clearly transition to the model architecture, detailing how it leverages this data to achieve structure-preserving editing via three key components: the Dual-Guidance Attention Block, Multi-Stage Feature Extraction, and Time-Adaptive Gating.

We will ensure the revision emphasizes the synergy between these parts—demonstrating how the dataset enables the specific architectural innovations of the model.


> **Q4: Applicability to Hunyuan3D 2.1 SoTA generative pipelines.**

**A4:** We appreciate the reviewer’s inquiry regarding the integration with recent SoTA models like Hunyuan3D 2.1. We analyze its applicability with respect to the two core components of our framework:

(a) Dataset Construction (Appearance-Driven Edits): Our current data generation pipeline relies on a Repaint-based strategy to ensure edit locality. This technique strictly requires a generator with explicit spatially structured latent features (such as the voxelized latents in Trellis ) to selectively update only the masked regions while freezing the rest. In contrast, Hunyuan3D 2.1 utilizes a vector-set latent representation which lacks direct spatial correspondence. Consequently, it is technically incompatible with region-specific repainting and cannot currently replace Trellis for constructing our paired appearance-driven dataset.

(b) Model Architecture (3DEditFormer): Conversely, our proposed model components, specifically the Multi-Stage Feature Extraction and Dual-Guidance Attention Blocks, are designed to be backbone-agnostic. Since they operate on standard attention mechanisms, they can, in principle, be integrated into any transformer-based 3D backbone, including Hunyuan3D 2.1. This would theoretically enable a "3D-Structure-Preserving Conditional Hunyuan3D". We view this as a valuable direction for future exploration. However, given the current inaccessibility of the Hunyuan3D 2.1 training code and the substantial computational resources required, we leave this specific adaptation for future work when the infrastructure becomes more accessible.

> **Q5: Missing related work on native 3D diffusion models.**

**A5:** We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We agree that native 3D diffusion models represent a significant branch of 3D generative modeling. In the revised version, we have expanded Section 2 (Related Work) to include a comprehensive discussion of these approaches.

Thank you for taking the time to review our rebuttal and for providing your follow-up comments. We are pleased to hear that our clarifications addressed your concerns. We truly appreciate your positive assessment and the effort you put into evaluating our work.

Thank you very much for your thoughtful follow-up and for increasing your score. We truly appreciate your positive evaluation. We will make sure to incorporate the detailed discussions into the final version of the paper to improve its clarity and soundness.

summary.value: This paper introduces 3DEditVerse, a large-scale paired 3D editing dataset, and 3DEditFormer, a transformer-based framework that preserves 3D structure consistency during localized editing. The dataset combines pose-driven geometric and text-guided appearance edits, while the model employs a dual-guidance attention mechanism and time-adaptive gating to disentangle editable and preserved regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved 3D editing performance compared with previous baselines.

strengths.value:
1. The overall pipeline is well structured, integrating dataset design and model development in a coherent way.

2. The generation process of 3DEditVerse is reasonable and clearly described. Although current edits are limited to addition/deletion operations without other types of edits, e,g., local deformations, this is acceptable since “editing” itself covers a broad concept.

3. The experiments are comprehensive and reproduce multiple baselines, showing consistent quantitative advantages.

weaknesses.value:
1. Could the framework be extended to support deformation-like edits, not just add/remove or appearance changes? Such capability would make the system more general and practically valuable.

2. There are two diffusion modules in Trellis (for voxel generation and structured latent modeling). Are both feature hierarchies actually leveraged in 3DEditFormer, or only one of them? 

3. How about the inference time consumption?

4. Minor one: the title emphasizes “Consistent”, but the paper does not clearly define or quantify “consistency” — is it geometric consistency, text-geometry alignment consistency, or temporal consistency across views?

**To Reviewer dgbA**

Thank you for the insightful and positive comments. In the following, we provide our point-by-point response and hope our response helps address your concerns. We also look forward to the subsequent discussion which further helps to solve the current issues.

> **Q1: Fairness of Comparison with VoxHammer.**

**A1:** We respectfully clarify that our evaluation protocol is designed to ensure fairness and applicability, rather than favoring our method. 

(1) Infeasibility of Mask-Based Methods for Pose-Driven Editing: Methods like VoxHammer fundamentally rely on a predefined, static 3D mask to anchor unedited regions while updating the edited area. However, in pose-driven editing (e.g., a character falling or crouching), the entire geometry undergoes global deformation, making it impossible to define a "local" static mask.

To validate this, we conducted an additional experiment where we treated the entire voxel space as the editing mask for VoxHammer (since the whole body moves). As shown in Appendix Fig. 13 (and the new analysis), without a static unmasked region to serve as a structural anchor, VoxHammer exhibits catastrophic geometric collapse and fails to generate meaningful results. In contrast, 3DEditFormer, guided solely by the target image without mask constraints, successfully reconstructs the deformed pose with high fidelity. This confirms that comparing mask-based methods on the Character-Animation subset is methodologically meaningless, necessitating their exclusion.

(2) Radius Inflation (Robustness): The "radius inflation" experiment is not meant to handicap the baseline, but to evaluate practical robustness. In real-world workflows, user-provided masks are rarely pixel-perfect. To validate this, we have added Figure 14 in Appendix. As visualized in the figure, VoxHammer is highly sensitive to mask precision: mask expansion (+9% to +27%) leads to severe artifacts, such as background erosion (e.g., holes in the floor) and geometric distortion. In contrast, our mask-free 3DEditFormer consistently generates high-fidelity results without requiring any auxiliary mask supervision, demonstrating superior stability for practical applications.

Crucially, even when VoxHammer is provided with masks with no "radius inflation", our method without such masks still outperforms it on 6 out of 7 metrics (Table 2). This confirms our superior performance is derived from the proposed method, not the evaluation setup.

> **Q6: Comparison with unified 3D generation/understanding/editing frameworks (ShapeLLM-Omni).**

**A6:** We appreciate the suggestion to compare with ShapeLLM-Omni. While it is a promising unified framework, we identify several structural constraints that distinguish it from our dedicated editing approach and currently prevent a direct empirical comparison:

(1) Limitation of Coarse, Geometry-Only Representation: ShapeLLM-Omni employs a 3D VQ-VAE that compresses data into discrete tokens representing low-resolution ($64^3$) binary voxels, explicitly discarding texture information. Consequently, the model's capability is restricted to coarse geometric reasoning. It cannot independently generate high-fidelity, textured 3D assets; instead, it relies on the external Sparse Flow Transformer (from Trellis) to hallucinate fine geometry and texture during reconstruction.

(2) Lack of Texture Understanding: Because the discrete tokens encode only voxel occupancy, the "understanding" module is blind to surface appearance, color, and fine-grained texture. This fundamental decoupling limits its ability to perform semantic edits that require joint reasoning over geometry and appearance.

(3) Editing Inconsistency: This separation between coarse voxel editing and texture reconstruction often results in misalignment. As illustrated in Fig. 6 of the ShapeLLM-Omni paper, the final output can exhibit inconsistencies where the high-frequency details and texture do not perfectly match the coarse geometric edits predicted by the LLM.

(4) Unavailability of Editing Weights: Crucially, as noted in the official repository, the model weights supporting multi-turn dialogue and 3D editing are listed as a future "TODO". The current open-source release supports only generation and understanding. Therefore, a direct quantitative comparison is currently infeasible.

In contrast, 3DEditFormer is conditioned directly on the edited target image, enabling precise, texture-aware, and structure-preserving modifications. We will include empirical comparisons once the relevant ShapeLLM-Omni weights are released.

Dear ACs,

We would like to respectfully underscore the fact that, prior to the OpenReview deanonymization incident, one reviewer had already raised their score based on our rebuttal and revisions: Reviewer MB98 from 4 → 6. In addition, Reviewers 41EE and En71 explicitly stated that our rebuttal, revisions, and video results on anonymous project page (https://anonymousresearch37.github.io/3DEditFormer/) had fully resolved their concerns, and therefore they maintained their initial positive assessments. **The overall scores before the incident were 6, 6, 6, 2.**

All of these post-rebuttal discussions and rating changes took place before the leak and the subsequent rollback, and the updates that motivated the higher scores have already been reflected in the current PDF and rebuttal: VoxHammer robustness analysis, evaluations on real, deformation, and non-human data, TAG stability analysis, inference efficiency comparison, data pipeline clarification, and expanded related work.

Although we greatly appreciate all reviewers' efforts, we would like to note that Reviewer dgbA (score = 2) raised several concerns that stem from misconceptions regarding both our evaluation protocol and established domain standards. **Notably, Reviewer dgbA's concerns stand in contrast to the consensus of the other reviewers:**

* On Experimental Validity: Our comparison protocol with VoxHammer was **clearly and explicitly articulated in the manuscript**, and the reviewer's claim (Q1) does not align with the procedure we actually used and documented. Moreover, Reviewer MB98 affirmed that **"the experiments are comprehensive, and the final performance clearly outperforms existing baselines,"** and Reviewer En71 similarly noted that our evaluation **"reproduces multiple baselines, showing consistent quantitative advantages."**

* On Experimental Settings: The comment regarding the use of clean, white backgrounds overlooks (Q3) the fact that such settings are **standard and widely adopted for 3D object editing**, as seen in EditP23, Instant3dit, and even VoxHammer itself. Crucially, **this setting was not raised as a concern by any other reviewer**, further confirming its acceptance as a standard convention in the field.

Our detailed clarifications on these issues are provided in the rebuttal. Unfortunately, **Reviewer dgbA did not participate in any post-rebuttal discussion**, preventing us from correcting these inaccuracies or providing further clarification.

We fully respect the decision to revert reviews for fairness and provide this note only to help the ACs interpret the present reviews together with the revised manuscript.

Best Regards, 

Authors

summary.value: This paper aims to advance 3D editing from both data and model perspectives. It introduces a large-scale paired “before/after” dataset called 3DEditVerse (claiming 116,309 training pairs and 1,500 testing pairs) and proposes 3DEditFormer, which builds upon the frozen Trellis image-to-3D generation framework by adding dual-branch cross-attention and temporal adaptive gating. The method claims to achieve localized and cross-view consistent editing without requiring 3D masks.

strengths.value:
1. The paper combines geometry-editing (pose-driven) and appearance-editing (text-guided) pipelines to produce paired samples with local and consistent changes at a larger scale than prior work.
2.  The idea of separating fine-grained structural features at late diffusion timesteps from semantic transition features at early timesteps is reasonable and clearly implemented through temporal gating.

weaknesses.value:
1. The comparison with VoxHammer seems unfair: for methods requiring masks, the authors remove subsets without character-animation masks, while for their own method, they report both full and subset results, including a favorable “radius inflation” test. The comparison setup benefits their approach.
2. The data pipeline depends on a chain of large pre-trained models (DeepSeek-R1, Flux, Qwen-VL, Trellis, SAM2), introducing heavy model bias and coupling—these models might appear again during evaluation, compromising fairness and generalization to real-world assets (complex backgrounds, non-centered subjects, lighting variations).
3. The use of clean, white backgrounds for stable lifting amplifies bias and limits applicability to realistic scenes. No real-scene qualitative results are shown.

questions.value:
1. Please summarize performance under occlusion, cluttered backgrounds, high-frequency textures (e.g., hair, wires), and topology changes.
2. How does the temporal gate behave across edit types (texture-only, geometry-only, mixed)? Any instability or gradient conflict observed?

comment.value: Thank you for your follow-up and for taking the time to review our additional experiments. We appreciate your evaluation and are glad that all your questions have been addressed.

summary.value:
The paper presents a complete pipeline for preparing 3D editing pair data, termed 3DEditVerse, and a novel 3D editing method called 3DEditFormer.
For the dataset, it consists of two parts: a pose-driven dataset and an appearance-driven dataset.
For the editing method, the authors propose a dual-attention mechanism that attends to both the semantic target image instruction and the fine-grained structural details of the source object.
Comprehensive comparisons with existing state-of-the-art 3D editing models demonstrate the effectiveness of both the proposed dataset and the method.

strengths.value:
1. This paper provides a data pipeline for producing 3D-consistent edited data pairs, which is an important contribution to this research area. The pose-driven part demonstrates strong 3D consistency since it is constructed using animation pose data. Although the appearance-driven part still has some limitations in 3D consistency, it achieves higher consistency compared to previous data generation pipelines.

2. The dual-attention module in 3DEditFormer is novel. It simultaneously considers both semantic information from the target image and fine-grained structural details from the source object, enabling the model to accurately edit the target regions while preserving the original geometric features.

weaknesses.value:
1. The pose-driven part of the dataset applies animation poses to characters, which makes it primarily applicable to human-like objects. Therefore, this type of structural editing is somewhat limited in scope.

2. The appearance-driven data generation pipeline appears overly complex, as it involves many modules and processing stages. Such complexity increases the likelihood of failure at each stage and makes the overall pipeline less stable.

3. The paper does not provide video results to verify whether the edits maintain good quality and align well with source objects and target image, which is particularly important in 3D editing.

questions.value:
1. There are other types of 3D editing beyond the pose-driven category, such as articulated-object or part-level editing, where ground-truth data could also be used to construct 3D edited pairs. Could the authors provide more discussion on the applicability of their data pipeline to these types of editing tasks?

2. The appearance-driven data generation pipeline appears quite complex, involving multiple stages:
(1) prompt generation, (2) source image generation, (3) edit prompt generation, (4) target image generation, (5) 3D pair initialization, (6) 2D and 3D mask computation, and (7) 3D inpainting.
Since each stage may fail and require manual filtering, could the authors report the success rate of each module as well as the overall pipeline?

3. Could the authors provide video demonstrations of the 3D editing results to better illustrate the consistency of the edits?

> **Q4: Performance under Occlusion/High-Freq/Textures/Topology Changes.**

**A4:** We conducted additional qualitative evaluations on these challenging scenarios, and the corresponding visualizations (Videos 6–10) are available on our anonymous project page: https://anonymousresearch37.github.io/3DEditFormer/ and Figure 12 in the revised Appendix.

(1) Topology Changes: 3DEditFormer handles substantial topological modifications effectively. Benefiting from the generative prior of the latent diffusion backbone, our model can add, remove, or reconfigure geometry to match the semantic target. As illustrated in Video 6 (bathtub → sink), Video 8 (crab → octopus), and Video 10 (turret → dragon head), the model reconstructs entirely new connected components while preserving global structure and edit locality.

(2) Self-Occlusion: Our method retains geometric and appearance coherence even in regions heavily self-occluded in the source. Video 7 (replacing the ice cream with a watermelon base) shows that textures on the back-facing and occluded surfaces remain consistent with the intended edit, demonstrating robust cross-view reasoning.

(3) High-Frequency Textures: 3DEditFormer successfully preserves and synthesizes fine-grained details such as thin structures, wires, fur, and sharp edges. As shown in Video 9 (mechanical arm with exposed wires) and Video 10 (dragon teeth and hair), the model maintains high-frequency textural identity despite large semantic edits.

Overall, these results confirm that 3DEditFormer is capable of handling challenging occlusion patterns, complex textures, and non-trivial topological changes with strong structural and appearance consistency.

> **Q5: Effectiveness of Time-Adaptive Gating (TAG).**

**A5:** To analyze the stability and behavior of the Time-Adaptive Gating (TAG), we categorized our test set into three subsets: Texture-Only, Geometry-Only, and Mixed Editing. We evaluated the performance with and without TAG.

| Editing Type | Method | PSNR ↑ | SSIM ↑ | LPIPS ↓ | DINO_I ↑ | CD ↓ | NC ↑ | $F1^{0.01}$ ↑ |
|-------------|--------|--------|--------|---------|----------|--------|------------------------|-----------|
| **Mixed** | w/o TAG | 26.003 | 0.934 | 0.0479 | 0.958 | 7.558 | 0.895 | 84.681 |
|           | w/ TAG  | **26.408** | **0.939** | **0.0442** | **0.962** | **6.965** | **0.902** | **86.247** |
| **Texture** | w/o TAG | 26.122 | 0.929 | 0.0474 | 0.955 | 6.385 | 0.922 | 85.408 |
|            | w/ TAG  | **26.131** | **0.932** | **0.0469** | **0.958** | **6.160** | **0.924** | **85.804** |
| **Geometry** | w/o TAG | 26.023 | 0.934 | 0.0501 | 0.960 | 8.488 | 0.897 | 83.837 |
|             | w/ TAG  | **26.503** | **0.938** | **0.0458** | **0.963** | **7.375** | **0.905** | **85.623** |

Across all three editing categories, the TAG-enabled model consistently outperforms the baseline. The results indicate that TAG provides uniform performance gains rather than favoring or harming any specific edit type. The above experiments have been added to the revised version

To further assess the stability of TAG, we monitored the training loss curves for both versions of the model (with and without TAG). As shown in Fig. 5 in the revised version, the TAG-enabled model follows a trajectory nearly identical to the baseline without oscillation or divergence. This confirms that introducing TAG does not introduce training instability, nor does it cause gradient-level conflicts between the semantic and structural guidance branches.

Thanks for the detailed discussion provided by the author. All my concerns are resolved and increased my score. Please remember to include those detailed discussions in the final paper to improve the soundness.

summary.value:
The paper introduces 3DEditVerse, the largest paired 3D editing dataset constructed via pose-driven and text-guided pipelines to ensure multi-view consistency and semantic harmony. It proposes 3DEditFormer, a transformer-based framework that utilizes Dual-Guidance Attention and Time-Adaptive Gating to achieve precise, structure-preserving 3D editing without relying on explicit 3D masks.
Initial concerns focused on the fairness of the baseline comparisons, the potential for error propagation in the complex data generation pipeline, and the method's limited generalization to diverse, real-world editing scenarios:
1. Reviewer dgbA raised significant concerns regarding the fairness of the comparison with the baseline VoxHammer, specifically criticizing the exclusion of mask-based methods from the pose-driven subset and arguing that the "radius inflation" tests artificially disadvantaged the baseline.
2. Reviewers dgbA, 41EE, and MB98 pointed out the potential for error accumulation and model bias in the data pipeline, as it relies on a long chain of foundation models, which might limit the diversity and realism of the generated data.
3. Reviewer dgbA challenged the method's reliance on clean white backgrounds, arguing that this setting amplifies bias and strictly limits the method's scalability to real-world, in-the-wild scenarios with complex environments.
4. Reviewers En71 and 41EE questioned the scope of the editing capabilities, noting that the pose-driven dataset is limited to human-like objects and asking for evidence of deformation-like edits beyond simple addition or removal.

The authors provided a comprehensive rebuttal that introduced additional evaluations on deformation-like edits, expanded the scope to non-human objects, and clarified the dataset construction process. Although Reviewers En71, 41EE, and MB98 were satisfied by these additions and recommended acceptance, the fundamental technical flaw raised by Reviewer dgbA regarding the fairness of the baseline comparison remains unresolved. Consequently, these methodological issues outweigh the contributions of the dataset size, leading to a recommendation of rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value:
1. The authors demonstrated that 3DEditFormer outperforms VoxHammer on 6 out of 7 metrics even when the baseline utilizes perfect ground-truth masks (0% inflation), and clarified that static masks are technically infeasible for global pose changes. The empirical evidence showing superior performance even under the baseline's ideal conditions strongly refutes the claim of a rigged experimental setup.
2. The authors detailed a rigorous filtering protocol (retaining <50% of data) and highlighted that ~46% of the dataset comprises ground-truth animation frames to counteract generative hallucinations. While synthetic data bias remains an inherent risk, the strict quality control measures were deemed sufficient by the majority of reviewers.
3. The authors clarified that neutral backgrounds are the standard for Mesh-based Single Object Editing (distinguishing it from Scene Editing) and demonstrated successful generalization on real-world scanned objects (GSO). The concern stemmed from a domain misconception (Object vs. Scene requirements), which was effectively clarified and validated by domain standards.
4. The authors provided qualitative demos for deformation edits and an inference time table showing efficiency comparable to EditP23. Reviewers explicitly confirmed that the additional experiments fully addressed their questions.

> **Q2: Data Pipeline & Model Bias.**

**A2:** We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding pipeline complexity. To strictly mitigate model bias and prevent error propagation, we employed a multi-faceted quality control strategy.

(1) Rigorous Automated Filtering (Appearance-Driven Pipeline): For the text-guided appearance edits, we implemented a strict filtering protocol at every stage, retaining only high-fidelity pairs:

* Prompt Generation: Starting with the 4,585-word Vocabulary Set from Tag2Text, we utilized DeepSeek-R1 to generate 20 diverse prompts per word, resulting in an initial pool of 91,700 text prompts.

* Image Generation & Editing: Source and target images were generated via Flux.1-Dev and Flux.1-Kontext, respectively. To filter out cases where the editing model failed to execute the instruction (resulting in near-identical images), we computed similarity scores and discarded pairs with negligible changes. (Remaining: 89,550).

* 3D Pair Initialization: Images were lifted to 3D using Trellis. Pairs where the source and target 3D assets remained identical in voxel space were removed, as they provided no useful geometric editing signal. (Remaining: 70,144).

* Mask Computation: We utilized Qwen-VL for edit localization. Samples where the model failed to detect a valid editing region (i.e., no bounding box returned) were discarded to guarantee successful 3D mask projection. (Remaining: 55,026).

* Consistency Filtering: Finally, we applied the Post-Editing Consistency Filtering (as detailed in Section 3) using multi-view DINOv2 similarity to eliminate inconsistent generations. (Final High-Quality Pairs: 43,874).

Consequently, the pipeline retains only 47.8% of the initial candidates, ensuring high reliability. Examples are shown in Figure 6 in the Appendix.

(2) Balanced Data Composition (Bias Mitigation): Crucially, our training strategy does not rely solely on generative data. Approximately 46% (54,000 pairs) of 3DEditVerse consists of Character-Animation Compositions. These pairs are derived from deterministic animation frames of rigged characters, providing "ground-truth" geometric transformations. Because this subset is inherently free from generative model hallucinations, it acts as a strong regularizer, preventing 3DEditFormer from overfitting to the specific biases or artifacts of the foundation models used in the appearance pipeline.

(3) Superiority Over Existing Datasets: Finally, 3DEditVerse significantly outperforms prior benchmarks in both data volume and quality (Table 1):

* 3D-Alpaca-Editing (52,532 train / 0 test): Is less than half the size of our dataset and suffers from poor consistency because it independently generates "before" and "after" assets.

* CMD (40,000 train / 50 test): Is limited in scale and lacks semantic harmony, as it constructs edits by naively concatenating unrelated 3D objects.

* Edit3D-Bench (0 train / 300 test): Provides no training data and only a small test set, limiting its utility for learning-based approaches.

In contrast, 3DEditVerse (116,309 train / 1,500 test) is the largest paired 3D editing dataset to date (roughly $2\times$ larger than the nearest competitor). It is the first resource to simultaneously guarantee massive scale, edit locality, multi-view consistency, and semantic harmony, establishing a reliable foundation for training robust 3D editing models.

> **Q3: White Backgrounds & Realism.**

**A3:** We wish to clarify the scope of our work compared to scene-level approaches.

(1) Object vs. Scene Editing: Our work targets Mesh-based Single Object Editing, distinct from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Scene Editing [1]. In the mesh/object editing domain, it is standard practice to process assets on neutral backgrounds (consistent with baselines like EditP23, Instant3dit, and VoxHammer).

(2) Generalization to Real Data: To demonstrate generalization beyond synthetic data, we evaluated our model on real-world scanned objects from the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) [2] and PartObjaverse-Tiny [3] datasets. Visualizations (videos 6-10 available at our anonymous project page https://anonymousresearch37.github.io/3DEditFormer/ and Figure 12 in the revised Appendix) show that 3DEditFormer effectively edits these real-world scans. 

[1] View-Consistent 3D Editing with Gaussian Splatting. In ECCV, 2024.

[2] Google Scanned Objects: A High-Quality Dataset of 3D Scanned Household Items. In ICRA, 2022.

[3] SAMPart3D: Segment Any Part in 3D Objects. In Arxiv, 2024.
Thank you for the additional experiments for clarification. I have no more questions. I will keep my original rating.

> **Q4: Utilization and applicability for other editing tasks.**

**A4:** We appreciate the insightful suggestion regarding the broader applicability of our work. We address this in two aspects:

(1) Integration of Articulated and Part-Level Datasets: We agree that existing datasets focusing on articulated motion or part decomposition provide valuable "natural" supervision for 3D editing. Recent works like PartGen [1] (part-level generation) and SINGAPO [2] (articulated part manipulation) explicitly model structural variations. These can be readily incorporated into the 3DEditVerse benchmark as additional subsets, providing ground-truth pairs for training models on precise kinematic or component-wise modifications.

(2) Generalizability of Our Generation Pipeline: Furthermore, our proposed data generation pipeline is inherently task-agnostic. The text-to-image-to-3D workflow can be seamlessly extended to these tasks by simply adjusting the instructional prompts (e.g., directing the model to "open the car door" or "enlarge the handle"). Crucially, our downstream modules (Edit-Region Localization, Multi-View 3D Mask Projection, and Latent-Space Repainting) operate independently of the edit semantics. They rely solely on visual differences between source and target views. Consequently, our framework can automatically localize and process articulated or part-level edits without architectural modification. We consider this a promising direction for future expansion of 3DEditVerse.

[1] PartGen: Part-level 3D Generation and Reconstruction with Multi-view Diffusion Models. In CVPR, 2025.

[2] SINGAPO: Single Image Controlled Generation of Articulated Parts in Objects. In ICLR, 2025.

summary.value: The paper presents (1) 3DEditVerse, a large paired 3D editing dataset (~118K train pairs, 1.5K curated test pairs) created via two automated pipelines (pose-driven geometric edits and a text-image-3D appearance-edit pipeline) and (2) 3DEditFormer, a conditional transformer that injects multi-stage structural features from a frozen image-3D backbone (Trellis) via a Dual-Guidance Attention Block and a Time-Adaptive Gating mechanism to preserve unedited structure during localized edits. The authors report large quantitative gains over several baselines and ablate key components.

strengths.value:
1. The proposed dataset and benchmark is very helpful in this field, and addresses a real bottleneck of supervised 3d editing.
2. Clear model idea addressing an important failure mode (multi-layer feature fusion, and gating mechanism for better local editing and globally preserve the details)
3. The experiments are comprehensive, and the final performance clearly outperforms existing baselines (mainly VoxHammer).
4. The proposed method is very practical to the 3d-aigc research and industry.

weaknesses.value:
1. The main issue lies in the dataset curation. Though the text-image and image-3D pipeline can facilitate generating a large amount of paired data, I wonder whether this is the right / proper solution for 3D editing, since it will definitely involve error accumulation in the data conversion. For example, can the dynamic 3d object (like dataset used in Diffusion4D, be directly used for 3d editing? No error accumulation will be involved in this way)
2. The writing is not very coherent, perhaps due to this paper introduces many components (dataset, benchmark, model pipeline, and so on). 
3. This method is based on trellis3d, and for SoTA 3D asset generative pipelines like Hunyuan3D 2.1, I wonder whether the proposed method can be still applied?

questions.value:
1. Some native 3d diffusion models discussions are missing in the related work, like 3DTopia-XL (cvpr 25), GaussianAnything (ICLR 25), and also vecset-based (3Dshape2vec, siggraph 23) baselines.
2. Another line of work that aims for unified 3d generation, understanding, and editing, e.g., ShapeLLM-Omni (NIPS 25). More discussions / comparisons with this line of work should be introduced. Though ShapeLLM-Omni does not introduce 3d editing yet, it is very straightforward following the 2D domain progress (gpt-4o, meta-query, and blip-3o).
